items.body:
Smiling C trail their Shams Dinn diamond with this bounty of Washington Go-Go picks from the short-lived Aset label’s Whax, Treo, and Latonya, all recorded and originally released c. 1986-88. Like the Shams LP, A Totally New Sound brims with pure soulful optimism and home-baked charm, but rather than early Arabic rap and ‘80s boogie, this one surveys a blindspot in most collections with some of the rarest and most special Go-Go Records in existence. 

All eight song were written by the Aset label’s in-house players, revolving song-writers Mbu Mbulu and O Jabbo, and includes their semi-released instrumental Skip, along with three beauties by the 11 year old singer Latonya which are almost worth entry alone, plus one wild one by the Whax duo, and three from Treo, the trio of Cathy Young, Delores Lidell and Linda Lawson.

Seriously, the Latonya tracks are what pop dreams are made of - precocious yet innocent, flush with colourful melodies and driven by that bustling Go-Go hustle, the super infectious Dance Time is a ready-made anthem, while Eyes Of A Child and We Will Teach The Adults weirdly also recall early ‘80s Belgian cold wave crossed with Langley Schools Music Project, or something.

The Aset Players’ Skip reveals the boogie mechanics under their pop hood, while Whax tend to the freakier side with a spot of Rick James-ian flair, and Treo’s close harmonies come out perfectly pop-wise in Demands Demands Demands, but Second Is Too Close and the forlorn romance of When Your Love Is Gone feels too weird to be pop proper, and that’s where the magick lies in this LP, between Aset’s mainstream ambition and a realness of expression that can’t be missed.

items.body:
Trane’s first album as bandleader surfaces on Craft Recordings’ guided reissue tour of classic jazz totems, spotlighting a vital period of modal jazz development from his years with the Prestige label, circa playing with Thelonious Monk and Miles Davis.

Recorded in May, 1957 and published in September that year, ’Coltrane’ marks the point when the great saxophonist began to transcend the acclaim of his peers for much wider recognition, with record sales numbers to follow suit. At the head of band including Red Garland on keys, Paul Chambers’ bass, Albert Heath on sticks, and Sahib Shihab’s baritone sax, Coltrane’s sound matures with a unique balance of smoky quintessence and modal experimentalism that would greatly inform jazz music in moving forward, outward.

That's all ideally illustrated on the daring modal suss of opener ‘Bakai’ with its switches between dervishing brass and angular rhythm to cooler stroll, and the contrast with its proceeding ‘Violets for your Furs’, and again in the closing couplet of ‘While My Lady Sleeps’ with its almost frenzied darts between the romantic and curiously exotic, and extended jazz-blues trip ‘Chronic Blues’.

items.body:
Weirder, wider, knottier and more hypnotic than its predecessors, L'rain's fourth album closes out her opening act with a vivid firework display of canny cultural references, considered observations and, most crucially, heartbreakingly beautiful songs. It's dumbfounding material, the kind of omnivorous, masterful gear that just doesn't come around often enough - a future classic, to put it bluntly, FFO keiyaA, Mabe Fratti, Dawuna, Dijon or even Broadcast.

There's an aura of comprehensiveness that surrounds 'fata morgana'. Taja Cheek has fully broken in her influences and inspirations at this stage and works without hesitation, painting out her experiences of a broken world with a level of insight that's so rare it's almost unparalleled. We already know that Cheek is a forensic listener; 2024's 'I Killed Your Dog' was a chunky "anti-break-up" album that met sorrow head-on with psych rock, indie, classic R&B and haunted folk references, while its predecessor projected Cheek's ambition, embedding shoegaze and ambient influences into a widescreen collage of avant-garde expressions. It wasn't fusion, exactly, it was Cheek's real-world experience - both as an artist and a high-profile curator - inked on thick, deluxe stock in illuminated letters. And the cycle that she began in 2017 with her tape saturated debut comes to a close with 'fata morgana'.

'I Killed Your Dog' was well aware of its lineage, recorded and produced with a level of detail that immediately put it alongside '70s avant-rock and R&B classics, so 'fata morgana' scratches away another layer, making deeper, odder connections. Even the brief 'rumors of light' is anything but throwaway, casually introducing Cheek's voice through a hailstorm of looped interference that's broken up by disarming bouts of silence. This doesn't only slickly establish the record's experimental credentials, it echoes the eerie 'Transmission' tracks on DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing'. "This is not a dream," a garbled voice memorably stated, and Cheek's utterances hint at the exact opposite, a choppy mess of backmasked syllables, coughs and hesitations that suggest we're being lowered into a surreal fantasy. Fairytale muted piano phrases appear in the distance and 'with time' materializes on the horizon, kinked by buzzing oscillations that blur time just slightly until Cheek's whisper-sung vocals sidestep into the candlelight. 

Already, it's Cheek's most enigmatic track, occupying the confounding spot between an acid-tweaked Laurel Canyon memory, a half-heard gospel standard and Wendy Carlos's iconic 'The Shining' score: beautiful, meaningful and effortlessly cinematic. And Cheek continues to paint outside the lines, concocting half-song 'blue' from tape-mangled brass loops and gunky drum improvisations that she scrapes into a seductive, hazed atmosphere underneath her reverberating chorals. It's tempting to reference shoegaze or dream pop; the end result is similar, texturally at least, but 'fata morgana' is comprised of hardier raw material: minerals crushed by hand from funk, spiritual jazz, reggae, blues and rock 'n roll. That's never more obvious than on the gorgeous 'july 5th', when smudged folk - mixed with screaming feedback and analog bleeps, of course - mutates into a jerky soundsystem banger in its final act, imagining what OutKast's 'B.O.B.' might sound like if Atlanta was swapped out for Kingston.

Then there's the brassy standout 'elmyra', an anthemic start-stop post-pop banger that's part 'Haha Sound'-era Broadcast and part Wire, distorted to a level that would terrify most green-gilled pretenders. All this, and we haven't even mentioned the album's dense, maximalist lead single 'Soulless Cycle', a track that begins with chattering, bit-crushed samples and double-time kicks and lunges towards its glittering, psychedelic wall of sound that stands as an apt metaphor for the melancholy cacophony of contemporary reality. Before the album's done, Cheek slides in a lysergic slow jam ('birthday') and a near-ambient darkjazz diversion ('church of no one'), reminding us that perseverance and resilience is still possible - preferable, in fact.

Seriously, it's one of those albums that reminds you why you started caring about music in the first place, a milestone that's both cognizant of its place in history and hyper aware of the current moment. So, so good.

items.body:
Dalhous's first demo collection, originally released on Blackest Ever Black back in 2015. RIYL Ekoplekz, Christ or Forest Swords.

Officially established by Edinburgh-based duo Marc Dall and Alex Ander in 2012, the name Dalhous was really just a formality - the duo had already been working on material together, under the name Young Hunting, for years. This is the era that's properly dredged up here, compiling the demos that Ander and Dall originally compiled for an Intergalactic FM broadcast, eventually dubbing it to tape to fill a gap after the release of 'Will to be Well'. And it's good material, especially if you're interested in tracking the project's evolution. Picking up where that other notorious Scottish electronic duo left off when they wrote 'Twoism', Ander and Dall are fascinated by the kind of moods that disappeared when VHS was traded up for DVD. Not completely in thrall to B-movie soundtracks and documentary themes, Dalhous prefer to muddle their sound with rusted industrial grot, amping up the distortion and making sure the beats fall neatly off the grid. At 21 tracks, it's a lot to plow through, but it's tidy listening if you've already exhausted the duo's proper albums.

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s hugely influential debut LP of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smoked out nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueur, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state.  So strong was the impact of the album on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

Proper, tracky, Chi-style budgers from the badboy Delroy Edwards, back to his vintage tricks on spiritual home L.A. Club Resource

The jakbeat is strong on this one, laid down direct and cruddy in the best sense with drum machines and  synths toiled into driving grooves that sound like they could have emerged during the mid ‘80s early years of house. Covering the spectrum of jakbeat flavours, he crosses from the title tune’s sultry swerve to hypnotic bass goop in ‘Put That’, cruising from the rude Adonis like keys of ‘Bring The House’ to a smart glimmer of FM synthesis smeared into ‘How’d You Do That’, and some Faces drums-style machine tickets on ‘Don’t Ya Know’, saving the punchiest tackle for the percolated funk and honk of ’Sweet Geese’, and dope nods to Gene Hunt on ‘House Blitz.’

items.body:
All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.

items.body:
Moving sideways from Warp to Domino, Simian Mobile Disco's James Ellis Ford challenges himself on his second solo full-length, crafting a set of Sakamoto-inspired synth pop from his hospital bed.

Ford's always been capable of producing pitch-perfect pop - his appearance on records from everyone from the Pet Shop Boys to Depeche Mode is a testament to that - but 'Lost in Another World' is a more personal affair. It was written and produced in hospital after he'd been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia last year, "on the ward between rounds of chemo." Thankfully his condition has improved - he posted earlier this month that he's got no more treatment in store - but the album stands as a vulnerable reflection of a difficult time. Ford describes it as a "pep talk", and it draws on some of his most enduring influences, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Japan, to channel its complicated tangle of emotions. 

On the opening track (and lead single) 'Overtones', Ford's voice hovers over plasticky rhythmelodic sequences and rubbery '80s drums and you'd be forgiven for assuming it's a lost city pop demo. Ford doesn't let the energy fall off, either, waltzing through slow-motion melancholia on the tentatively beautiful 'Here Today' and John Foxx-style synth pop on 'This Too Shall Pass'. Ultimately, it's surprisingly hopeful material, infused with genuine feeling.

items.body:
Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.

Recorded last year, 'Lynboril Linsinopril' is a lengthy session from seasoned improvisers Adam Bohmen (on strings and amplified objects), Sue Lynch (on woodwind) and Crystabel Efemena Riley (on percussion).

All members of London's Horse Improvised Music Club, Bohmen, Lynch and Riley are motivated by the act of playing, something that's evident immediately. There's a refreshing freedom to their approach; it's relatively straightforward free improv gear, with Riley's tuff rhythm section providing an anchor for her collaborators' wildest skronk-y expressions, but breathes outside of the usual boundaries, never falling into the expected locked grooves. If you follow Cafe Oto's orbiting improv scene, this'll be worth a closer look.

items.body:
Scoring a graphic novel based on a dream he had in 2024, John Carpenter gets the band back together, turning in an album that'll delight fans of 'Lost Themes'.

We know full well that Hollywood doesn't seem interested in making Carpenter's films a reality any more - he's said as much, quite publicly. So what's the next best thing? Well, a graphic novel. 'Cathedral' was written by Carpenter alongside his wife (and long-time creative partner) Sandy King and, like all great Carpenter projects, it had to have a home-brewed score to ease it along. So who better to make the dream a reality than his regular bandmates Cody Carpenter and Daniel Davies? Chronologically, this one fits in right after 2024's 'Lost Themes No. 4: Noir', but fans of Carpenter's earlier (eerier) biz will be happy to hear that he's reaching a little further back this time. 

There's of course the hard rock influence that's been present since at least 'They Live', but every so often there's a glimmer of the earworm-laden synth pop that elevated 'Escape from New York', and the iconic 'Assault on Precinct 13'. Just peep the 'Halloween'-style piano breakdown on 'Inside Out', the 'In the Mouth of Madness' mood on opener 'Primeval' or the classic horror flex of 'Abandoned Cathedral', with its organs, orchestral swells and all-important Mellotron choirs.

items.body: In July, Europe was grappling with extremely high temperatures and, as a result, thunderstorms due to the heat dome over the continent. I live on the top floor of an apartment building and therefore had a particularly privileged view of these natural spectacles. On one occasion, I could see such a storm approaching - a dark wall rapidly pushing toward the city - though it was obvious that the weather front would only graze the city. The gusts of wind were fierce, trees bent under the force of nature, thunder roared, and lightning lit up the sky. But why am I telling you this? Because it fits perfectly with “Equilibrum”, the first track on the new album by the international trio Okuda Müller Hall - Rieko Okuda (Japan; piano), Matthias Müller (Germany, trombone), and Samuel Hall (Australia, drums) - perfectly. At first, the drums just tingle softly; Hall rubs the toms and strokes the cymbals, while Müller delivers an unsettling drone that shifts only slightly. Sometimes it grows louder, then fades again; it literally fluctuates. Then the piano slowly enters the picture, with Okuda attacking the interior of the instrument. Almost imperceptibly, everything grows louder, darker, and more menacing. The thunderstorm is now over you, but only a few heavy drops are falling, symbolized by isolated piano notes. Even though you know you’ll get off lightly, a hauntingly beautiful, fascinating feeling lingers. “Six Lights,” the third and longest track on the album, continues this form of improvisation in a similar vein. Müller, however, forgoes the drone, opting instead for deliberate, sustained notes over which Okuda showers bright piano sprinkles, while Hall works his magic on the dark drums and simultaneously manipulates extended materials. Müller then takes a two-and-a-half-minute break, and when he rejoins the piece, it actually sounds like contemporary European free jazz or like - say - a trippy ECM recording. In general, ³√ (“Cube Root”) combines wide-ranging developments with a finely balanced structure, it’s a perfect showcase of Berlin’s Echtzeitmusik scene, the trio’s music flows organically into a distinct sonic language - multi-layered, crystal clear, a combination of density and openness. The liner notes mention that an “acoustic space of great depth and fluidity unfolds, within which a steady pull develops, drawing the listener ever deeper into this flowing, ever-changing soundscape“. My favorite track on the album, though, is the last one, “Sputnik.” The thunder and lightning of the opener are gone; what remains is the wind - rough, wild, hissing around the corners and producing strange sounds. Rieko Okuda creates a powerful soundscape against which Müller and Hall enjoy a great deal of freedom, and which ultimately proves what they are - in a musical sense: a force of nature. The album ends with a few subtle dabs of piano. Fascinating and stunningly beautiful. ³√ is available as a download. You can listen to the cording here: ³√ by Okuda Müller Hall Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute, bass flute; Liberty Ellman: acoustic guitar; Jose Davila: tuba, trombone; Christopher Hoffmann: cello; Elliott Humberto Kavee: drums. I dig Henry Threadgill’s type of sound, how he orchestrates modern classical, progressive chamber jazz, and avant-garde opaqueness using layers that unfold with meticulously planned coherence and originality. Threadgill’s prominent presence on the contemporary avant-garde landscape has a strong association with Zooid, a tight quintet that has never felt so loose as in Cut You Where You Was . Threadgill is not heading into a new direction here, but the album has plenty to discover and enjoy. On “ Fluoroscope ”, we notice intervallic leaps within a highly contrapuntal environment, which is so characteristic of the saxophonist’s style. With a tight focus on arrangement and composition, the piece also counts on mystifying solos by Threadgill, who uncorks atypical melodies, and guitarist Liberty Ellman, whose acoustic patterns sound just right over the textural oddities generated by cellist Christopher Hoffman, tubist José Davila, and drummer Elliott Humberto Kavee. The three-movement chamber piece “ Bingo ” explores a variety of exquisite feels and moods: “ Bingo Part 1 ” sets elated flute flights against tuba wails, low-key guitar specifications, and somber cello; “ Bingo Part 2 ” features Ellman’s bluesy slide technique as flute and trombone contribute to the exotic, picturesque landscape; and “ Bingo Part 3 ” thrives on motivic alto sax and enthralled mallet drumming. “ Red Admiral Red Moon Rising ” is the album’s centerpiece, clocking in at more than 12 minutes. What begins as a mournful dirge with plenty of delightful detail quickly evolves into a captivating, quirky groove that has its own imaginative way of swinging. Only Threadgill can come up with these rhythmic jaw-droppers, and his dissonant solo here resonates within that narrative thrust. His ability to go against structural norms and jazz conventions is also mirrored on “ Off And On What Happened ”, where the inventive, unaccompanied Kavee shines. Counterpoint and fragmented cadences are injected before the skillful drummer finishes what he had started. “ Lightnin’ ” is another miniature gem, with sax and guitar declaring curious lines in unison and a deliciously offbeat groove underpinning Ellman’s clear yet nonconformist statement. Passion and openness are present throughout the album, and the final result is simultaneously haunting and bewitching. Favorite Tracks: 04 - Bingo Part 3 ► 05 - Red Admiral Red Moon Rising ► 07 - Off And On What Happened ► 08 - Lignin’

items.body:
For anyone paying attention to Vietnamese or Cambodian pop culture, the past several days have seen a flurry of online commentary in Southeast Asia and beyond about a new music video by Phương Mỹ Chi and DTAP titled 'Thiên đường với người thương', or 'Paradise with my love'. The track is in Vietnamese and follows the conventions of Vietnamese pop, but the music video (MV) features Khmer Krom culture from southern Vietnam, with scenes filmed at Khmer wats (temples), displays of Khmer dance, and a staging of a Khmer wedding. The central characters in the video are a classical dancer, played by Phương Mỹ Chi, and a musician, played by actor Bảo Định, who meet as children, grow up together, fall in love, and get married.

The video presents a wholesome story and celebrates Khmer Krom culture. The Khmer Krom, or lower Khmer, live in the Mekong Delta and are related to the Khmer people of Cambodia. Both were once part of the Khmer Empire, but several factors have shaped a distinct Khmer Krom culture. Starting in the 17th century, Vietnamese populations moved into the Mekong Delta, which ushered in several centuries of cultural mixture. French colonisation and independence movements established a boundary between Cambodia and southern Vietnam that limited movement. And the distinct qualities of the Mekong Delta itself yielded new cultural forms. The Khmer Krom therefore have many folk traditions about which little is known.

Responses to the video have largely been positive, but it has touched a nerve among some netizens who decry the cultural appropriation of Khmer culture by a Vietnamese pop artist. This debate offers insight into the wider geopolitics of Southeast Asia and the trends of contemporary pop in Vietnam.

The release of 'Thiên đường với người thương' has taken place amid vibrant experimentation with folk traditions in Vietnamese popular music. Songs of folk pop or folktronica feature pop singers reclaiming various folk traditions of their parents and grandparents to fuse them with popular music models that circulate worldwide. Phương Mỹ Chi has several tracks that blend southern Vietnamese traditional music with global pop aesthetics. Artists from northern Vietnam do the same: Hoàng Thùy Linh's 'Để Mị Nói Cho Mà Nghe' incorporates elements of Hmong music, and Kiều Anh's 'Lá Ngọc Cành Vàng' folds a short ca trù (sung poetry) tune into an instrumental interlude.

At the same time, the Vietnamese government plays an influential role both publicly and behind the scenes in promoting some artists over others. For instance, in 2013, the government banned public lip-synching to promote genuine vocal performance but later rescinded the ban. More recently, several pop musicians, including Miu Lê and Phương Diễm Huyền, faced criminal prosecution for supposed illegal activity. Any arrest is a warning to other singers, as Vietnamnet recently indicated.

In this context, Vietnamese pop artists must figuratively walk several tightropes in their artistic creation. The first tightrope involves navigating the razor-edged distinction between cultural appropriation and legitimate experimentation in an environment of fickle social media trends and youth tastes. On this, 'Thiên đường với người thương' has done rather well.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by VietQ Media (@vietqmedia)

An article in Cambodia-based The Phnom Penh Post suggests that the music video appropriately “acknowledges” the origins of the Khmer dance and rituals. This echoes Cambodian and Khmer Krom social media posts that relay a sense of pride in seeing Khmer culture represented on an international stage. Vietnamese and diasporic Vietnamese communities also enjoy the video, as VietQ Media has reported.

Social media posts strengthened the case for visual acknowledgement one day after the MV’s release. Phương Mỹ Chi gave her thanks to Trà Vinh University and her dance teacher, Thạch Thị Út Linh, while DTAP released a visual of musical instruments and customs seen in the music video.

The track has not been entirely successful in raising awareness of Khmer Krom sonic culture, however. During one instrumental interlude, for instance, the MV shows musicians playing various instruments of the Khmer classical music genre pinpeat, or ngũ âm in Vietnamese, including the sralai (a quadruple-reed instrument) and Bảo Định playing the roneat ek (xylophone). But the soundtrack contains none of the distinct timbres of these instruments. Instead, listeners hear a rather boring guitar riff. Khmer culture is seen here but not heard.

The second tightrope involves navigating opaque areas of government permissibility. I have no access to specific information about the making of the MV, but the video's wide circulation suggests that it meets government regulations and requirements. The song also upholds the ideals of the recent Resolution 80 on the development of cultural industries in Vietnam, which seeks to promote culture but also manage it appropriately.

Given this environment, it’s no small feat to find fertile middle ground between artistry and policy to successfully represent Khmer culture in Vietnam. This is of paramount importance because of the difficulties today in accessing Khmer Krom music, dance, and rituals. Artists do not often perform outside of the Mekong Delta, with only a handful of performances taking place every year in large cities in Vietnam. Tourists also rarely visit Khmer communities in southern Vietnam, given the lack of infrastructure.

At the same time, murky restrictions often prevent the study of Khmer arts in southern Vietnam. Earlier this year, the very university that supported the MV’s production team would not authorise my Khmer music lessons with staff instructors. This is, of course, the university’s prerogative, and given the long history of colonial and other forms of exploitation, I understand their caution. But my case is not an isolated one among domestic and foreign researchers in Vietnam. And might the commercial use of the Khmer arts by a Vietnamese pop singer also be seen as a form of exploitation?

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Phương Mỹ Chi (@phuongmychi)

The case of 'Thiên đường với người thương' is therefore a complicated one. The song acknowledges, represents, and values the Khmer arts in Vietnam, but at the same time manages and exploits them for commercial and nationalistic ends. But no government can fully control a narrative.

Among the online discussion are several commentators from Thailand who have both congratulated Vietnam for displaying “Thai culture” — thereby completely erasing Khmer and Khmer Krom culture — and remonstrated with Vietnam for featuring “inauthentic” forms of Thai costume and dance. In the midst of a military conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, they have added to the widening culture war between the two countries by bringing Vietnam into it.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ben Pham (@bnphm0609)

Pop is never boring, and foreign (i.e. non-Southeast Asian) audiences must start to pay attention to the dynamics that bring these songs to life. 'Thiên đường với người thương' encourages reflection on the interconnected nature of music and everyday life and the shifting tightropes that all individuals must navigate when making artistic decisions. And while certain powers may attempt to control a narrative, the openness of the Internet quickly dissolves that enclosure.

I am therefore optimistic about 'Thiên đường với người thương'. I truly hope that it will generate new interest in Khmer Krom culture and open new doors for Khmer artists to showcase their artistry to new audiences. The paradise of the video, then, may not be romantic love, but may instead be a paradise of visibility. Audibility may well be next.

Written by Alexander M. Cannon. He is Professor of Ethnomusicology at the University of Birmingham. This article benefited from a conversation with an avid consumer of Vietnamese popular culture who wishes to remain anonymous. Their contribution is gratefully acknowledged.

Fans who missed out on tickets to BIGBANG’s sold-out Singapore concert have another shot at catching the K-pop icons live.

Marina Bay Sands (MBS), an official sponsor of the BIGBANG 2026-2027 WORLD TOUR < XX : COSMOS > IN SINGAPORE on 17 October, has unveiled dining and hotel packages that come with Category 1 tickets to the group’s National Stadium show.

The BIGBANG Comeback Celebration

For fans looking to turn the concert into a getaway, The BIGBANG Comeback Celebration starts from S$3,800, with rates varying depending on stay dates.

The package includes:

2 Category 1 tickets to BIGBANG's Singapore concert

2-night stay in a Sands Premier Room for up to 2 guests

Stay period from 15 October to 23 December

Bookings are now open and can be made by calling Marina Bay Sands at +65 6688 8888 between 8AM and 8PM.

The Concert and Connoisseur Package

Starting from S$1,388, The Concert and Connoisseur Package pairs two Category 1 concert tickets with a curated dining experience for two.

Fans can choose from four Marina Bay Sands restaurants: Maison Boulud, KOMA, CUT, or Mott 32.

The package went on sale to eligible Paiza members at 3pm on 14 August. All Sands LifeStyle members can purchase the package from 12PM on 17 August.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AEG Presents Asia (@aegpresentsasia)

General-sale tickets to BIGBANG's Singapore concert reportedly sold out within two hours of going on sale on 13 August after overwhelming demand. Official tickets were priced from S$158 to S$498.

The Singapore date forms part of BIGBANG's 20th-anniversary world tour and marks G-DRAGON, TAEYANG, and DAESUNG's long-awaited return to the country.

For more information and to book the dining package, visit Marina Bay Sands' official BIGBANG world tour page.

Both packages are now sold out.

items.body:
ILLIT have released a Korean version of 'I Got Your Back', featuring BLACKPINK star JISOO and MOMOKA of HANA.

'I Got Your Back (Feat. JISOO, MOMOKA of HANA) (Korean Ver.)' brings the song's reassuring message — that "you are not alone" — to a bright rock backdrop of guitar riffs, dynamic drums, and a driving bassline.

The track was originally released in July as the lead single from ILLIT's second Japanese single and served as the main soundtrack for ABEMA original drama The Vacation Principle. It went on to peak at No. 2 on the Billboard Japan Hot 100.

Speaking about the new rendition, ILLIT shared: “‘I Got Your Back’ reflects our honest thoughts and emotions, so we focused on conveying that sincerity through our vocals. While it’s the same song, singing it in Korean gives it an entirely new feel.”

JISOO and MOMOKA, who also appeared on the original Japanese version, return for the release and wrote their own rap verses.

ILLIT are next set to continue their sold-out PRESS START︎ tour, with stops in Hong Kong and encore shows in Incheon and Chiba later this year.

items.body:
YEONJUN has unveiled the music video for 'Fxxking Star'. The new visual sees the TOMORROW X TOGETHER member turn up the intensity with an explosive approach that contrasts the sleek and refreshing mood of his last single, 'Ice Cream'.

'Fxxking Star' is taken from YEONJUN's latest solo album, NO LABELS: PART 02, with the music video offering another look at the confidence and individuality behind his solo work.

The release arrives amid YEONJUN's extensive run of solo activities in the U.S. The K-pop star recently performed at Good Morning America's Summer Concert Series in New York and the Z100 Summer Bash Presented By Wells Fargo, before heading to Los Angeles for an intimate Billboard: One Night Only performance at the Troubadour.

At the Troubadour, YEONJUN performed 'Vanilla', 'Ice Cream', 'Baby What's Up', 'Long Way Long Ride', and 'Fxxking Star', before closing the night with an encore of 'GGUM'.

He also took part in Korean Heritage Night at a Dodgers game, where he threw the ceremonial first pitch and delivered a live performance.

YEONJUN also made his solo debut at KCON LA 2026 on 15 August, before reuniting with TOMORROW X TOGETHER as the festival's headlining act the following day. The group is also scheduled to perform at the Global Citizen Festival in September.

The perception is that they were completely inescapable, having become an essential thread in the fabric of pop immediately. However in 1975, in the UK at least, they may have appeared to be circling the drain.  Having arrived in the European consciousness 18 months earlier with ‘Waterloo’, the positions of their subsequent releases in Britain were not initially encouraging. The levelling success of their Eurovision-powered number one, propelled their first British single, ‘Ring Ring’ from 1973, finally, up to the modest heights of Number 32, but the follow up proper that November ‘So Long’ bypassed the charts... items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Rarely has a transitional album been so significant, not only for the band's own history but also for the evolution of the genre. The search for roots hinted at in previous albums deepened on Unhalfbricking; indeed, the cover photo features Sandy Denny's parents standing in front of their Wimbledon home, with the band seated in the garden behind them. "Genesis Hall" features a strange blend of Celtic tradition and psychedelic elements, but the standout feature is Sandy Denny's voice, ethereal, as if swaying in the wind, which was a fundamental part of the band's classic era. Country influences also contributed to a cohesive whole where backing vocals and electric instrumentation, played by young musicians performing melodies with ancient roots, combined to create a unique sound.Since Richard Thompson, like Simon Nicol and bassist Ashley Hutchings, also sang in addition to playing guitar, Sandy's lead vocals, backed by them, created an intimate and warm atmosphere for the songs, such as "Si Tu Dois Partir," which benefited greatly from the switch to French. That dreamy quality Sandy brought to her singing, reminiscent of a day by the sea, is palpable in "Autopsy." The track's jazzy percussion complements the band's harmonic richness; midway through, the rhythm shifts and settles into a steady groove, prompting a change in her vocal delivery. They were experimenting and blending genres in their own way, incorporating an electric guitar solo, supported by the second guitarist, that straddled the line between blues and jazz.After its long introduction, "A Sailor's Life" launches into a jam that blends Indian ragas with Celtic tradition as if they belonged to the same region; yet when the band breaks into psychedelic rock improvisations, Sandy recedes into the background, for she was no Janis Joplin (and I adore Janis), and she always maintained her composure. Fairport Convention was her Big Brother & The Holding Company, and the two guitars (much like in Jefferson Airplane) freely take flight, connecting invisible points to form yet another constellation among the stars."Cajun Woman" leans towards rock 'n' roll, followed by "Who Knows Where The Time Goes?", a song composed by Sandy Denny, where time itself seems to stand still under the spell of her voice, which remains undiminished. "Percy's Song" begins with a collective, a cappella harmony from the entire band, and when the electric dulcimer and drums join in, that shared spirit, that sense of communion, is further strengthened."Million Dollar Bash" closed out the album, featuring the rhythm of regional ballroom dances and an energetic frontman; the track's rhythm is paradoxically electrifying, despite being predominantly acoustic and driven by guitar, bass, and drums, as it blends Celtic harmonies with rock 'n' roll elements once again. I think that, beyond their inherent talent, one of the keys was that they were young people of the 60s with their own influences... playing music from eras long past, even from before they were born, where written and oral traditions merged just as the music did. Many eras coming together to form an era beyond time.

items.body: Review by svetstawniichuk — I came to this album after Dedication To BigNick, knowing it was a different kind of letter. Quia Nesciunt Quid Faciunt is the eleventh studio record, the third for Lizard, and the first and last full studio album with Evgeny Trefilov, who left just before it was finished. The Latin title means they know not what they do. The band say it was induced by the military operations and human-rights violations of recent years. Most of the pieces were composed in the late 2010s and lived on stage between 2018 and 2021; the extra recording, mixing and mastering ran to 2023. They also say the message sits most clearly in The Man Whose Wings Were Cut Off. I tried to hear the record that way: not as a collage of older live tunes, but as one long argument about people who act without knowing the cost.Bait of Success does not wait. In the first forty seconds Rozmainsky's harpsichord and synths are already locked to Semenov-Tyan-Shansky's guitars, Kirillov's bass and Trefilov's drums ? and those drums really do lean toward progressive metal, as the credits warn. Korotkikh's flute sits in the mid-high line rather than decorating the edge. The first two minutes keep slamming doors (loud blocks around 0:12?0:41, then 0:57?1:20, then a peak near 1:56). Then the floor drops. From about 2:00 to 3:10 the kit and the low end almost leave the room; what remains is a thinner keyboard and guitar weave, as if the bait had been taken and the room emptied. Around 3:10 the band returns and holds a long last-third wall until the last ten seconds simply stop. Trumpet is named as an essential melody voice of the whole album, not of this track alone, so I will not pretend I can timestamp Gorshkov bar by bar. I hear a bright brass colour inside the denser passages and leave it there.Daybreaking is warmer and more even. The centroid sits lower; the volume barely jumps around. This is one of only two pieces that credit Korotkikh's low whistle, and you feel that immediately ? a wooden, slightly folk breath under the harpsichord instead of a silver flute edge. The first minute and a half stay mid-range. After about 1:03 there is a short cut, then the group rebuilds. The real climb is the middle: from roughly 2:22 to 4:16 Trefilov and Kirillov push a single long loud block, the peak sitting near 4:15. After that the high end thins, the drums keep walking, and the last twenty seconds fade. No clarinet here, no guest bass. It is the core five, with that low whistle as the extra colour.Fountain is a minute and a half of Trefilov's synth piano. Rozmainsky's synths are credited everywhere except this miniature and the closing Nocturne, and you can hear the difference: a soft, low-centred keyboard room, almost no sparkle above 1 kHz, no kit taking the lead. A small crest around 0:24, another near 1:06, then it dissolves. I did not skip it. It is a pause the album needs.Se Camminiamo Nella Luce (LP Version) is the only track with Rozmainsky's grand piano, and again one of the two with low whistle. For the first hundred seconds it stays private ? piano, keys, a restrained guitar, almost no drum wall. Just after 1:44 the floor opens and the full group arrives at once. From about 2:04 to 4:45 the piece is a long bright walk; there is a brief hole around 3:30?3:42, then the loudest stretch of the track, peaking near 4:29. The last twenty seconds thin out. The Italian title says if we walk in the light. The arrangement does that literally: two minutes in shadow, then almost four in the open.Premonition is the longest piece, just over nine minutes, and the most consistently loud once it decides to speak. The first minute is a held breath ? the quietest second of the whole track is the opening. Around 1:05 the band steps in, and from 2:04 to 5:19 it barely lets go. Trefilov's kit is a motor here, not a commentator; Rozmainsky's harpsichord keeps cutting through the guitar midrange; flute lines appear in the brighter layers. After 5:30 the pressure drops, the last three minutes walk rather than climb, with a few late pulses around 8:05?8:50. If the album has a long warning, this is it. I hear no guest clarinet and no slide guitar ? the official sheet keeps those for later ? and I will not invent them.Walking is the strangest shape on the record, and the only piece that credits Rozmainsky's metallophone. The first two minutes are already bright and busy (high centroid, a lot of high-frequency chatter). Then, just after 2:07, the bottom falls out: a hole of almost a minute where the drums and the bass almost vanish and the midrange hangs in the air. At about 3:10 the group slams back, and the last two minutes are the loudest ? the peak sits at 5:06, almost at the end, as if the walk had been uphill the whole time. The metallophone is not a solo; it is a hard, bell-like glint inside the keyboard layer. I kept replaying the hole. That silence is the point.Wides does the opposite of Walking. It holds a mid-loud floor for two and a half minutes, then from 2:31 to 4:32 it becomes a single wall ? peak at 4:00 ? then it steps down, then it builds a second wall from 5:30 to the last four seconds. Core band again: Kirillov, Trefilov, Semenov-Tyan-Shansky, Rozmainsky, Korotkikh. No guests. The title fits. The piece is wide more than it is deep; it occupies the room and does not leave.The Man Whose Wings Were Cut Off (LP Version) is where the record changes its clothes, and it is the piece I will keep. Kirillov steps aside; Lokosov takes the bass. Liubcenco comes in on guitars, rubab and doira; Luniov on ukulele; Perevalov on clarinet ? the only tracks with clarinet are this one and the next. The first forty seconds are almost empty. Then the guests arrive in waves: a first lift around 0:50, a harder one at 1:23, and the loudest crest of the album near 2:23. The middle keeps folding ? thirteen separate loud sections, the brightest and noisiest spectrum on the record ? and after about 6:00 the floor drops again into a long, thinner coda of clarinet, keys and those dry folk colours (rubab, doira, ukulele) until the last half minute almost whispers. The band never played the short 2020 single on stage. This longer LP version feels like the reason. If the title of the album is an accusation, this track is the wounded figure in the middle of it. Favorite, without a contest.Beautifulness (LP Version) keeps the same guest room ? Lokosov, Liubcenco's guitars, Luniov's ukulele, Perevalov's clarinet ? and adds the only slide guitar on the album. It does not wait the way track 8 waited. The first half minute is already open, there is a second crest around 0:44?1:10, a dip, and then the peak from 2:37 to 3:14. After 3:20 the high end leaves and the last twenty seconds fade. Where Wings was an argument, this is the aftertaste: same players, softer shoulders.Nocturne closes as Fountain opened the inner door: Trefilov's synth piano, no Rozmainsky synths, a low-centred minute and twenty seconds. A small crest near 0:29, then it goes. Two miniatures as bookends around a record that otherwise hits hard.I will not pretend this is a chamber album in the Dedication sense. Trefilov's drums keep the long tracks in a rock room, the harpsichord is almost a lead guitar, and the two guest pieces at the end change the folk and woodwind colour completely. The two keyboard miniatures will be skipped by some listeners. I did not skip them. Taken as a letter about people who do not know what they are doing, the record holds together. Four stars from me ? excellent, and the one I will return to when I need the title explained in notes rather than in words.Favorite track: The Man Whose Wings Were Cut Off (LP Version).

items.body: Review by svetstawniichuk — I came to this album already knowing it was not just another Roz Vitalis studio record. It is the first one they have given to a single person: Nikolai Bogaichuk, BigNick, the producer and publisher who loved music the way some people love a second country. He died in 2023. The band write that he once dreamed of putting out their best album, and that these pieces were recorded and mixed by different hands at different times, yet the record is not a compilation. It is a concept album about the creative path of a man with an endless love for music. I tried to hear it that way.The Tragedy of The Ancient Spring (Extended Version) opens the door slowly. For the first half minute I mostly hear Rozmainsky's piano and synths with Perevalov's clarinets, then the air opens and I can pick out Korotkikh's flute and Gorshkov's trumpet ? the only track where those two are credited, and you feel that immediately. Semenov's drums do not rush in; they arrive around the forty-second mark and start to give the chamber writing a pulse. The middle is a long climb. Somewhere past three minutes the bass of Lokosov and the drums sit under a denser weave of keys, guitar and woodwind, and the last big wave holds for about a minute before the piece thins out and almost dissolves. Chichagov's and Semenov's sound effects sit in the grain rather than waving at you. It is a dedication that does not shout.Captivated (Atmospheric Version) begins much quieter, almost like a held breath. For the first minute the picture is mostly keyboards ? organ-like synth, a hint of harpsichord ? and then Liubcenco's guitar and Trefilov's drums pull the room into focus. The brightest stretch sits in the middle of the track, where clarinet lines and those dry, slightly folk-tinted strings (rubab, doira) keep crossing the piano. There is a short dip around four and a half minutes, as if someone opened a window, and then the band comes back until the last half minute fades. I like how little it tries to impress. It just stays in the air.Target (LP Version) is the album's most sudden piece. The first forty-five seconds are almost private: keys and clarinet in a narrow mid range, no real drum kit. Then a second layer arrives, and just after a minute and a half Trefilov's drums and the bass slam the door open. From about 1:36 to 2:16 the track is a wall ? the loudest single block on the record ? then it steps down, then it builds again toward the end. No trumpet or flute here. What I follow is clarinet, piano, bass, drums, and Rozmainsky's keys changing the temperature of the room.Teach Me Thy Statutes (Part 1) is thirty-four seconds of grand piano. Nothing else really sits in the low end. It is a sketch, a question left on the table.Loneliness-Bringing Power is the piece I keep going back to. It is the quietest of the long tracks, and it barely changes its volume, which makes every colour count. From the first bars there is a deep bass and a sliding line ? Luniov's slide ukulele, credited only here ? against bass clarinet and harpsichord. For a long time Trefilov holds back. The drums become obvious only in the last two minutes, when the weave tightens and then lets go. The title could have been a pose; instead the music really does feel like strength that has gone quiet on purpose. If I have to name a favourite, this is it.Teach Me Thy Statutes (Part 2) returns to the same piano idea and lets it grow for a minute and a half. After the halfway mark a single mid register is held almost like a pedal, and the last fifteen seconds are the most forceful. Still no drums, still no bass guitar. Two small rooms of piano around the heart of the album.The Threesunny Light Power (Very Abridged Version) starts as a slow, organ-coloured keyboard piece with almost no high sparkle. Around the two-minute mark the colour flips: piano, a lighter midrange, and then, toward the end, the bells Rozmainsky is credited with on this track only. You can hear them as long ringing lines after about 3:30, when the rest of the band has already stepped aside. No drummer is listed here, and I do not hear a kit taking the lead. Olga Grigorieva mixed this one; it has a different air from the heavier tracks.Resilience (Expanded Version) waits almost a minute in a thin keyboard haze, then the full group arrives at once. This is the loudest piece on the album, and the only one with Kirillov's bass instead of Lokosov. Semenov is back on drums. Clarinets and keys carry a melody that keeps folding back on itself; later there are high sweeps that feel like tape or synth rather than a cymbal wash. The last forty seconds thin out again. I hear a life that keeps starting over, which is probably more than the notes asked for, but the title allows it.Silence Is Waiting (Thy Statutes Version) is the goodbye. Piano and long synth pads, Semenov touching the drums in the middle rather than driving them, and then, after about three minutes, the low end simply leaves. What remains is a mid drone that gets quieter until there is almost nothing. Chichagov mixed this one with the first track, and the two bookends feel related: one opens a room, the other closes it and leaves the light on.I will not pretend this is a rock album in the usual ProgArchives sense. It is chamber music with a rhythm section that comes and goes, and two piano miniatures that some listeners will skip. I did not skip them. Taken as a letter to one man who loved this band, the record holds together. Four stars from me ? excellent, and close enough to their best work that I will keep it near the player.Favorite track: Loneliness-Bringing Power.

items.body: Review by Nickmannion — Firstly it would be great if someone could edit my 'guess who didn't check it through before pressing send' error. I missed out the fifth and integral to the sound member of the band, the fabulous Jack Lancaster on sax and sometimes other horns. Much appreciated.Secondly I stumbled across a site that was a history of the Marquee Club (London) a few years back. For non UK PA regulars, it was THE venue in London from about 1966/7 to 1976/7 ish where all aspiring prog and related bands wanted to play. Out of curiosity I started checking random weeks line ups and hit on the idea of having a Marquee night as in play an album from each band on that week. Yup, the first week I found where I had an album/s from the whole line up was early 1972 and of course it is my way in to say the Mick Abrahams Band were one and they encapsulate what we might call a cold wet Thursday eve gig/sound at the Marquee. Some may shrug shoulders, others may groan...but for me it was the dogs clacker bags....although being a northerner and only 12 at the time of the week in question, it was retro heaven. Mick was a bluesman and by this time had long since burnt off any 'ex Jethro Tull' kudos and possibly Blodwyn Pig too. Nope he was not a straight down the line Savoy Brown Years After kinda guy, as some of the extended heavier work outs on the first MAB album show, but it was his influence. I have mentioned this before but back then, blues rock and blues based bands were considered 'progressive'. I don't know why that seems to have dissipated, especially here, but it is what it is. So with the second MAB album we have the 'heavy' knob on the Marshall turned down a fair bit from the first lp and also the sax element gets more prominence. Similar sounds? A touch of Colosseum and If, a bit of Man actually and I hear some Mott The Hoople too. The opener shuffles along nicely till an amazing free jazz squall of a sax solo and then slows into a two chord funky lope that allows a distortion free guitar to fill the spaces. Absent Friends is very Chicago/Ten Wheel Drive horn rock and unsurprisingly very 'American' sounding. The next track hints at Lindisfarne, which may be a mandolin thing. Whole Wide World could be a Skin Alley track but it does swing rather than the leaden thud of the mentioned comparison. Maybe Because is 'the long one' and only works in the second half when keys/sax/guitar get chance to wig out. The ideas and changes in the first half are a bit clunky 'shall we still try to be prog or not' compromises. Up and Down is the most riff laden track and reminds me of something from a Skid Row (as in the Gary Moore power trio) album. You'll Never Get It From Me coulda been a Faces song.So, there you have it. As early '72 a Marquee band album as you could wish for. I prefer the first MAB release but as I submitted this entry for the album, I went with this for a review. A solid 3 stars if you care to widen narrow prog tastes and in researching this I had missed the news that Mick passed last December. Rest easy big man.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — England's Windmill Scene has single handedly put the UK back on the map for innovative progressivemusic by spawning 21st century sensations such as Black Midi, Black Country New Road and Squid. Thisnew style has kept prog relevant and innovative in the 2020s when most prog bands tend to drift moretowards retro band worship than anything truly revolutionary. Unsurprisingly the modern progsmorgasbord style that features a cocktail of math rock, post-punk, noise rock, avant-prog and jazzhas taken the world by storm and with Chile coming of age in recent years, it's also not a shock tofind an intrepid act from Santiago offering some new freshness to the world of progressive music.HESSE KASSEL only formed in 2022 but quickly made a splash with its debut release 'La Brea' in 2025which offered a rather Godspeed You! Black Emperor style of post-rock in cahoots with bouts of artpunk, the frenetic chaos of noise rock and the controlled angularities of avant-prog. While thealbum showcased a crafty new form of fusion, the album tended to drift on in a nebulous swirl ofpost-rock infused atmospheric overload for much of its 78-minute playing time which resulted in arather lopsided roller coaster ride of sheer exhilarating energetic overdrive amidst long bouts ofaimless ambient swirling about. However it didn't take long for this sextet to get the memo andreturns in 2026 with MORIR SALTANDO (Dying While Jumping) which carries over the best qualities ofthe debut and jettisons the boring parts.A much more streamlined effort, MORIR SALTANDO features six tracks at a nice digestible near 45-minute excursion through the band's signature crossroads where progressive rock, post-punk, jazz,noise rock and post-rock convene for a little powwow of sorts. The results have yielded one of thebest albums that has emerged in the calendar year 2026 and demonstrating why Chile has become one ofthe most exciting hotbeds of musical talent in recent years. The album instantly grabs yourattention with the feisty 'Pornomiseria' which builds tension with an opening metronomic drumbeatbefore lead vocalist Renatto Olivares offers some excellent narrative rap and roll dialogue inSpanish albeit with the demeanor of a punk rocker that moves on to noisy punk guitar counterpointsand emphatic backing vocal outbursts. The track serves as the epic multi-segmented opener that spansthe course of over 14 minutes through various movements that demonstrates the band's fiery andpassionate instrumental interplay.'No Me Puedo Relajar' features a shorter more punk-infused condensed playing form firing on fullpistons and high octane for its entirety while 'El Reflejo' reverts back to some of the post-rockleanings of the debut album albeit set to an indie rock song form however at eight minutes alsoshowcases the band's seamless flow between musical motifs and creative cadences that somehow flowtogether surprisingly well. While the band nails the incitable noisy post-punk references, the bandis equally adept at infusing more contemplative moments with beautiful piano parts and jazzysaxophone performances. 'Mariposa' demonstrates perfectly why the album holds together so well as itcontinues the art of changing up dynamics, tempos and compositional prowess in fine form. Using ahigh speed clean guitar tone riff as its opening basis the track undergoes a unique metamorphosisthrough varying stylistic effects that deliver the band's uncanny ability to fuse punk and jazz withprog and calamitous noise.Despite the more artistic excursions, HESSE KASSEL delivers a more traditional anarcho-punkthrowback with 'Sancho Plagio,' the same style that opens the album reminding me of classic Crassbut just as you think you're in for some Chilean anarchy the track breaks into some sort of art jazzrock excursion! But the genius of this band is how they can alternate between two distinct stylesrather seamlessly while maintaining the underlying rhythmic backbone and melodic flow. The albumends with 'Tulpa' which offers the last dose of jazzy punk art prog with noise-infused regalia. Wow!This is a huge step up from 'La Brea' and the band doesn't miss a beat with its expansiveprogressive sound that firmly remains rooted in that DIY indie ethos. An amazing feat to bridgethese two extremes but this album sounds perfectly mixed, recorded and constructed. It pretty muchshowcases everything a progressive punk rocker could possibly want. Probably the best thing sincethe Cardiacs if you ask me. Don't miss this one!

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Safe As Milk" is the debut full-length studio album by US, California based music artist CaptainBeefheart (released under the Captain Beefheart and his Magic Band moniker). The album was releasedin August 1967 through Buddah Records. The Magic Band was formed in 1964 by guitarist Alex St. Clairbut when lead vocalist Don Glen Vliet joined in early 1966 the name was changed to Captain Beefheartand His Magic Band. The Magic Band would eventually become the backing band of Vliet but most futurealbums would still be released under the name Captain Beefheart and his/the Magic Band. CaptainBeefheart and his Magic Band were initially signed to A&M Records and released the two singles"Diddy Wah Diddy" and "Moonchild" for the label. But when it became time to record "Safe As Milk",A&M Records dropped the band as they felt they didn�t have the commercial potential they werelooking for. Hence "Safe As Milk" was released through Buddah Records. The material on "Safe As Milk" is blues oriented rock with an occasional psychedelic edge but alsowith traces of folk rock and rhythm & blues. Vliet�s raw voice and expressive singing style is thedominant feature of the music, but the heavy blues rock rhythm section, Ry Cooder�s organic leadguitar work, and Vliet�s harmonica playing are also ingredients of the album�s soundscape. It�s araw and organic sound which suits the band�s skills and performance style well. All tracks are relatively short (between 2-3 minutes long) and there are few experimental excursionsinto avant-garde rock territories which Captain Beefheart would soon be known for. "Electricity" andmaybe "Dropout Boogie" being some of the exceptions with a slightly more experimental songwritingapproach. In that respect "Safe As Milk" is overall a pretty straight forward blues rock/rhythm�n�blues oriented album. The album is well produced featuring an organic and detailed soundproduction. The mono recording style sometimes feels a bit odd today with the vocals not beingcentered in the mix, but there is a charm to that too. A 3 star (60%) rating is warranted.

items.body: Review by Alxrm — The band was not under my radar until 2023 when Spooky... came out and while listening to internet stations some of their songs captured my attention. There were many reasons for that. To begin with, the orchestrations are rich, inspired and very intelligent, using an astonishingly wide variety of instruments. There are also abundant time changes that flow naturally and each song is built upon numerous themes, each giving way to the next smoothly and as a result they sound perfectly coherent. They possess all the strong points progressive music can have while simultaneously it is accessible and relatively easily digestible. The vocals are pure delight to listen to and the lyrics are carefully and intelligently put together, On top of that, the production is crystal clear allowing each instrument to shine.The only track that hasn't grown on me is the epic He Once Was and I mean not totally since there are many solid parts in there, it just doesn't keep my interest intact all the way. Also the bonus track There Goes My Baby isn't among the best, yet although the title sounds a bit inane, the song actually isn't. Overall, it is a very feel-good album where the songwriting is the primary focus and not the technical show-off, but still there are many details to discover. A textbook example how to make accessible, but genuine progressive music.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Compositions built on enchanting crescendos, pronounced post-metal progressions with a lush, cinematic foundation; an invitation to journey through the atmosphere, to levitate to the rhythm of the catchy instrumental. A linear post-rock sound."Archons" opens with a spacey, cinematic intro, a contemplation of music from the heavens, from space, launching into "Moon Machine," which shifts in moments from post-rock to post-metal with its shimmering guitar reverb over Zack's staccato drums. Three guitars converse amongst themselves with an air reminiscent of The Cure, the chorus reprising the familiar style of inviting guitars while surfing on a dark, strange new-wave sound. "Sea of Glass" stands out for its dark yet luminous melody built on loop pedals and delay, an oxymoron. The melancholic atmosphere illuminates the radiant guitars, reaching deep into our ears, which are set ablaze by this overwhelming sonic onslaught. "Blurry Creatures" features a western-elegiac choir, an anthemic chant accompanying the celestial pounding of the percussion. The build-up is one that Anathema wouldn't disown, with its sharp riff, ethereal choir, and those signature musical delays amplifying the haunting sound of this contemplative melody."Silence Between Mountains, Pt. 1" opens with an arpeggiated intro, the electric guitars adopting an acoustic approach; a shimmering, meditative, radiant melancholy of the diptych leads into "Silence Between Mountains, Pt. 2," a dark, languid, sad, and beautiful track. An addictive, endless repetition of notes acts like an echo within our ears. The shattering dub, with its explosive sound, swells and flirts with the distress of the guitars on "28 Days Later," desperate and despairing. The heavy riff amplifies the atmosphere before the subdued acoustic outro. "Metanoia" features a sharp rock riff, a moment where the guitars converse in stereo, the cold wave sound taking hold before the pronounced shearing that brings a cascade of emotion. The first of the three short tracks showcases the lead guitar solo. "Flim" opens with a solemn, colorful sound, momentarily dispelling the established grayness. An electronic sound, heavily influenced by Aphex Twin, creates an atmosphere that is both solemn and playful. This tribute, coupled with a legacy, allows the sun's rays to shine through. "Endlessly Connected" follows with radiant, incisive guitars; a slow, deliberate progression to be taken as a captivating and enchanting final interlude.IF THESE TREES COULD TALK creates a luminous post-rock universe, using Zack's drums as a catalyst, Jeff, Mike and Cody's guitars as a musical will-o'-the-wisp and with Tom as the metronome.
